notes.body:
All of detection is conditional probability, so we start with the foundations and make them operational. A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes; an event is a subset. P(A) is the fraction of the space where A happens. Conditional probability P(A|B) — 'probability of A given B' — is the fraction of B-outcomes where A also holds: P(A|B) = P(A∧B)/P(B). Worked: a SOC sees 10,000 network events; 200 are port scans (event S), and 50 of those come from external addresses (event E∧S). P(E|S) = 50/200 = 0.25 — a quarter of scans are external. Note the direction matters: P(S|E) — 'given external, how many are scans' — is a different number requiring the count of external events. Confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) is the prosecutor's fallacy wearing a SOC badge: '99% of intrusions trigger this alert' (P(alert|intrusion)) is not '99% of alerts are intrusions' (P(intrusion|alert)) — the second is what the analyst needs, and it is usually far smaller. Independence: A and B are independent if P(A∧B) = P(A)P(B) — knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Worked: two independent sensors each with 1% false-positive rate. P(both false-positive) = 0.01×0.01 = 0.0001 — independent corroboration multiplies confidence, which is why defense-in-depth stacks independent signals. But verify independence: two signatures from the same vendor on the same engine are not independent — correlated sensors give correlated failures, and the multiplication is a lie. The law of total probability partitions the space: P(A) = P(A|M)P(M) + P(A|¬M)P(¬M) — 'alerts come from malicious events plus benign events,' the denominator you will need for Bayes. Common mistake: treating 'rare' as 'never.' A 0.1% event across a million daily events happens a thousand times a day. Scale converts rarity into routine — the fundamental reason SOC math surprises newcomers.

The prosecutor's fallacy deserves its own worked autopsy because it recurs in incident response. Setup: 1% of employees are malicious insiders (prior). A UEBA tool flags 90% of malicious insiders (P(flag|malicious) = 0.9) and 8% of benign employees (P(flag|benign) = 0.08). An employee is flagged. P(malicious|flag) = (0.9 x 0.01) / (0.9 x 0.01 + 0.08 x 0.99) = 0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0792) = 0.009 / 0.0882, about 10.2%. The tool is '90% accurate at catching insiders' and the flagged employee is roughly 10% likely to be one. Presenting the 90% number to HR as the employee's guilt probability is the fallacy — and it ruins lives when the base rate is ignored in personnel decisions. The correct presentation: 'the flag raises the probability from 1% to 10% — investigate, don't accuse.' Every detection number you report must survive this translation: what was the prior, what is the posterior, and what action does the posterior justify? Investigation thresholds and accusation thresholds are different numbers, and Bayes tells you which is which.
notes.title: Probability foundations for detection

notes.body:
Bayes' theorem is the single most important equation in security operations: it converts 'how good is the sensor' into 'how much should I believe this alert.' P(M|A) = P(A|M)·P(M) / P(A), where P(A) = P(A|M)P(M) + P(A|¬M)P(¬M). In words: posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence. The prior P(M) is the base rate — how often malicious events occur. The likelihood P(A|M) is the sensor's true-positive rate. The denominator counts all alerts, true and false. Worked — the IDS example, every number shown. Setup: 1% of events are malicious (prior P(M)=0.01). The detector catches 99% of malicious events (P(A|M)=0.99) and false-alarms on 5% of benign events (P(A|¬M)=0.05). An alert fires. How likely is it real? Numerator: P(A|M)·P(M) = 0.99 × 0.01 = 0.0099. Denominator: 0.0099 + P(A|¬M)·P(¬M) = 0.0099 + 0.05×0.99 = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594. Posterior: 0.0099/0.0594 = 1/6 ≈ 0.1667. Sixteen point seven percent. A '99% accurate' detector produces alerts that are real one time in six — because the 5% false-positive rate applies to the 99% of traffic that is benign, generating far more false alerts than the 1% malicious base generates true ones. Frequency form, same result, more intuitive: 10,000 events → 100 malicious, 9,900 benign. Detector flags 99 of the 100 malicious and 5% of 9,900 = 495 benign. Total alerts: 594. Real: 99. 99/594 = 16.7%. Teach the frequency form to stakeholders; keep the formula for yourself. The lesson: sensor quality (likelihood) and alert believability (posterior) are different things, joined by the base rate. Every 'why are all our alerts false positives' complaint is Bayes' theorem asking to be noticed. Common mistake: quoting the true-positive rate as the alert's credibility. P(A|M)=99% does not mean the alert is 99% likely real — that confusion is the base-rate fallacy, next note.

Bayes composes: each new piece of evidence updates the posterior, which becomes the next prior. The IDS alert took us from 1% to 16.7%. Now a second, independent sensor — say, a sandbox detonation — also flags the file, with its own 90% TP and 5% FP. Update: prior 0.1667, posterior = (0.9 x 0.1667) / (0.9 x 0.1667 + 0.05 x 0.8333) = 0.15 / (0.15 + 0.0417) = 0.15 / 0.1917, about 78.3%. Two mediocre sensors in agreement: 78% — the independence multiplies the evidence. (Verify independence before multiplying: two signatures from the same engine don't count twice.) This is the mathematical form of 'corroborate before you escalate': each independent confirmation should move your belief by a computed amount, not by vibes. In practice, run the SOC on posterior tiers: single-sensor alerts get automated enrichment, two-sensor agreement gets analyst review, three get immediate escalation. The tier boundaries are posterior thresholds you have computed, not alert counts someone guessed. And log the updates — when the post-incident review asks 'why did you escalate,' the answer is a chain of Bayesian updates, each with its numbers. That is defensible triage.
notes.title: Bayes' theorem, worked on IDS alerts

notes.body:
The base-rate fallacy is ignoring the prior — and in security, the prior is always tiny, so ignoring it is always catastrophic. Restate the IDS result as a fallacy autopsy: the analyst hears '99% detection rate, 5% false positives' and feels the alert is ~99% likely real. The actual answer is 16.7%. The missing ingredient was the base rate: malicious events are 1% of traffic, so the false positives (5% of the huge benign mass) swamp the true positives (99% of the tiny malicious sliver). Now scale it to a real SOC and watch it get worse. Worked: 1,000,000 events per day, 10 real attacks (base rate 0.001%). Same excellent sensor: 99% TP, 1% FP. True alerts: 10 × 0.99 = 9.9. False alerts: 999,990 × 0.01 = 9,999.9. Total: ~10,010 alerts per day, of which ~10 are real. Precision: 9.9/10,009.8 ≈ 0.099% — one alert in a thousand is real. The sensor is superb and the alert stream is 99.9% noise. This is not a sensor problem; it is arithmetic. Operational consequences, in order of leverage. First, tune thresholds per environment: the vendor's default threshold was set for their demo data, not your base rate — measure precision on your traffic and move the threshold until the alert volume is triageable. Second, stack independent signals: two independent 1%-FPR sensors ANDed give 0.01% FPR on the combination (independence permitting), which is how you dig out of the base-rate hole. Third, enrich before alerting: an alert with asset context, threat intel, and corroborating logs is a different (higher-prior) population than a raw signature hit — tier your response by posterior, not by sensor output. Fourth, accept the math publicly: tell stakeholders 'our IDS alerts are 15% likely real, which is why every alert gets corroboration' — managing expectations beats apologizing for false positives. Common mistake: 'fixing' the base-rate problem by buying a 'more accurate' sensor. Going from 99% to 99.9% TP barely moves the posterior; cutting the false-positive rate in half doubles it. When base rates are tiny, false-positive rate is the only metric that matters.

The base rate is not a single number — it varies by population, and stratifying is free precision. The 0.001% base rate was across all events; but among events already flagged by a coarse pre-filter, or from high-risk assets, or during an active campaign, the prior is much higher. Worked: take the SOC example but restrict to alerts from the finance VLAN during a known phishing campaign — suppose the prior there is 2%. Same sensor (99% TP, 1% FP): posterior = (0.99 x 0.02) / (0.99 x 0.02 + 0.01 x 0.98) = 0.0198 / (0.0198 + 0.0098) = 0.0198 / 0.0296, about 66.9%. Identical sensor, 0.1% to 67% believability, purely from a better prior. Operationalize this: tier your alerting by population priors — exec assets, crown-jewel servers, and campaign-targeted groups get lower thresholds because their base rates justify it; the general population gets higher thresholds. This is also why threat intel matters mathematically: intel doesn't just add detections, it raises priors on specific populations, making every sensor more precise there. 'Context' in SOC-speak is often just 'a better prior' in statistics-speak — and now you can compute exactly how much better.
notes.title: The base-rate fallacy in alerting

notes.body:
Precision, recall, and F1 are the working vocabulary for evaluating any detector — learn them as ratios on the confusion matrix, not as slogans. The matrix: rows are ground truth (actually malicious / actually benign), columns are the detector's verdict (flagged / not flagged). Four cells: TP (true positives — caught badness), FP (false positives — false alarms), FN (false negatives — missed badness), TN (true negatives — correctly ignored). Precision = TP/(TP+FP): of everything flagged, how much was real — the analyst's 'is this alert worth my time' number. Recall = TP/(TP+FN): of all real badness, how much was caught — also called true-positive rate or sensitivity. FPR = FP/(FP+TN): of benign events, how many false-alarmed. Worked on a concrete matrix — TP=90, FP=30, FN=10, TN=870 (1,000 events, 100 actually malicious). Precision = 90/(90+30) = 90/120 = 0.75. Recall = 90/(90+10) = 90/100 = 0.9. F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) = 2(0.75)(0.9)/(0.75+0.9) = 1.35/1.65 ≈ 0.818. F1 is the harmonic mean — it punishes lopsided tradeoffs: precision 1.0 with recall 0.01 gives F1 ≈ 0.02, exposing the 'flag nothing, be precisely right' cheat that accuracy would hide. (Accuracy here would be (90+870)/1000 = 96% — sounds great, misses 10% of attacks.) The tradeoff is fundamental: lowering the threshold catches more (recall up) but alarms more (precision down, FPR up). There is no threshold with both perfect — the detector's quality is the whole tradeoff curve, which is the ROC of the next note. Choose the operating point economically: estimate the cost of a false positive (analyst minutes) and a false negative (breach risk), and pick the threshold minimizing expected cost — not the threshold maximizing F1, unless your costs happen to be symmetric. Common mistake: reporting accuracy on imbalanced data. The M25 vendor demolition ('99.9% accurate, 0% recall') is the canonical example — accuracy is the metric you quote when you want to hide the tradeoff.

Choose the metric by the decision it informs. Tuning a threshold? Watch precision and recall move against each other and pick the economic optimum. Comparing two detectors for purchase? Compare full ROC curves, not single points — a detector that wins at your operating region is what matters. Reporting to leadership? Precision ('what fraction of analyst hours were well spent') and alert volume, because that is the budget they feel. Hunting false negatives? Recall on a labeled set, because precision is silent about misses. Debugging a bad week? The confusion matrix itself — which cell grew tells you what changed (FP spike means benign traffic shifted or the threshold drifted; FN spike means the attacker adapted or there is a coverage gap). And never let anyone optimize accuracy on your imbalanced data — the vendor demolition stands. One more: when classes are imbalanced, also report the raw counts alongside ratios. 'Precision 0.75' could be 3/4 or 750/1000 — the ratio is the same, the evidence behind it isn't. Ratios summarize; counts justify. Give both, always.
notes.title: Precision, recall, F1: reading the confusion matrix

notes.body:
A ROC curve shows the detector's entire tradeoff surface: true-positive rate (recall) on the vertical axis versus false-positive rate on the horizontal, traced as the threshold sweeps from 'flag everything' (top-right: TPR=1, FPR=1) to 'flag nothing' (bottom-left: 0,0). A perfect detector hugs the top-left corner (TPR=1 at FPR=0); a random detector is the diagonal (flagging at random catches badness exactly as often as it false-alarms). Real detectors bow toward the top-left, and the area under the curve (AUC) summarizes the bow in one number: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is coin-flip. Worked intuition with the synthetic example from your lab: benign scores cluster around 0, malicious around 2 (both with spread 1). At threshold 1.0 you catch most malicious (high TPR) with moderate false alarms; at threshold 3.0 you almost never false-alarm (low FPR) but miss much malicious (low TPR). The ROC is the curve connecting these operating points — and moving the threshold slides you along it, never off it. Two honest uses. First, comparing detectors: if detector A's ROC is everywhere above B's, A is better at every tradeoff — no threshold games can rescue B. If the curves cross, the 'better' detector depends on your operating region (low-FPR region for SOC triage, high-TPR region for pre-breach hunting). Second, choosing the operating point: mark your cost ratio on the curve — the optimal threshold is where the marginal true positive is worth the marginal false positives. AUC's honest limit: it averages over all thresholds including absurd ones (FPR=0.9 is not an operating point anyone uses), so for SOC work, partial AUC over the low-FPR region is the serious metric. Common mistake: 'our model has 0.99 AUC' as a deployment argument. AUC measures ranking quality across thresholds; your deployment lives at one threshold, on your base rate, with your costs. Report the confusion matrix at the operating threshold — AUC is the trailer, not the movie.

For imbalanced detection problems, the precision-recall (PR) curve is often more honest than ROC. ROC's FPR uses true negatives in the denominator — and when benign events number in the millions, the FPR stays tiny even with thousands of false alarms, making the ROC look deceptively good. The PR curve plots precision vs recall directly: it shows what the analyst experiences (how much of my queue is real?) at each recall level. Worked intuition: our SOC sensor at 99% TP and 1% FP has a fine-looking ROC point (TPR 0.99, FPR 0.01 — near the top-left!) but a PR point of (recall 0.99, precision 0.001) — the PR curve exposes the operational reality the ROC hides. Rule of thumb: balanced classes, use ROC; imbalanced (the security norm), use the PR curve, with area under the PR curve as the summary. Report both when comparing detectors, but make decisions on the PR curve at your operating region. And the same threshold economics apply: pick the PR point where marginal costs balance. The curve changes; the decision method doesn't. Metrics are lenses — choose the lens that shows the thing you are deciding about.
notes.title: ROC curves: the full tradeoff picture

notes.body:
Detection also needs counting statistics: how many events to expect, and whether today's count is weird. Two distributions cover most operational questions. The binomial counts successes in n independent yes/no trials: P(exactly k) = C(n,k)·p^k·(1−p)^(n−k). Worked: 100 logins, each independently 1% likely malicious. P(at least one malicious) = 1 − P(none) = 1 − 0.99^100 ≈ 1 − 0.366 = 0.634. A 1% per-login risk becomes a 63% certainty of at least one bad login in a hundred — scale converts rarity to routine again, the quantitative backbone of 'assume breach.' Expected count: n·p = 1. The Poisson counts events in continuous time or space when they occur at a constant average rate λ, independently: P(k events) = e^(−λ)·λ^k/k!. Worked: port-scan probes arrive at λ=2 per hour. P(0 in an hour) = e^(−2)·2^0/0! = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135 — a quiet hour happens 13.5% of the time, don't celebrate. P(5 in an hour) = e^(−2)·32/120 ≈ 0.036 — five probes in an hour happens 3.6% of the time by pure chance; investigate, but know the base rate of 'weird-looking' hours. The Poisson's signature property: mean = variance = λ. If your observed counts vary much more than λ (variance ≫ mean), the process isn't simple-Poisson — it's bursty or clustered, which itself is signal (botnets beacon in bursts; humans don't). Operational uses: set alert thresholds from the distribution ('alert when hourly count exceeds the 99.9th percentile of Poisson(λ)') instead of from gut feeling; size log pipelines from expected rates plus headroom; and sanity-check vendor 'anomaly' claims — an 'anomalous' burst with 5% Poisson probability is Tuesday, not an incident. The two distributions connect: binomial with large n and small p approaches Poisson with λ=np — the 100-logins example (λ=1) gives P(0)=e^(−1)≈0.368, matching the binomial 0.366. Common mistake: alerting on counts without a rate model. 'Unusually many' is not a finding until you've computed what 'usual' looks like.

The variance check deserves a worked example because it is a detector you can deploy tomorrow. You monitor DNS queries per minute to a rarely-used internal resolver: historical mean lambda = 4 per minute. Under Poisson, variance should also be about 4 (std about 2). This week you observe minute-counts: mean 4.2, variance 38. Variance far above mean — not Poisson. Something is bursty: maybe a misconfigured retry loop, maybe DNS tunneling exfiltrating in bursts. The check caught what the mean missed (the mean barely moved). Formalize it: track the index of dispersion (variance divided by mean); alert when it exceeds, say, 3 for sustained windows. This is a real, deployed technique — simple, explainable, and sensitive to exactly the shaped traffic attackers generate (beacons, bursts, retries). Caveats: legitimate burstiness exists (batch jobs, cron storms) — baseline per-asset and per-hour, and confirm with a second signal before escalating. But as a cheap first-pass anomaly screen over count data, variance-versus-mean is one of the highest-value statistics in the module. It also generalizes: whenever a model assumes a distribution, check the moments. Models fail at the assumptions, and the assumptions are checkable.
notes.title: Binomial and Poisson: counting events like an operator

notes.body:
Close the loop: turn the statistics into a detection-quality program you can run. Four practices. One — characterize every detector with a confusion matrix measured on your data, at your operating threshold, refreshed regularly. Not the vendor's matrix, not last year's matrix: yours, now. Track precision, recall, and F1 over time; a drifting F1 is the earliest warning that the threat landscape or your traffic mix moved. Two — hunt your false negatives deliberately. False positives announce themselves (analysts complain); false negatives are silent. Sample closed-as-benign alerts and re-investigate a random subset deeply; sample raw event streams the detectors never flagged and hunt manually. Estimate the miss rate with a confidence interval and report it alongside precision — a detector with 90% precision and unknown recall is half-characterized. Three — price your thresholds. For each detection tier, write down the cost of a false positive (analyst triage minutes × volume) and the cost model of a false negative (expected breach cost × probability the miss matters). Set thresholds where marginal costs balance, and re-price when volumes change — a threshold that was optimal at 1,000 alerts/day is wrong at 10,000. Four — evaluate like a scientist (M26's experiment discipline applies to detectors too): any new detection logic ships with a baseline comparison, pre-registered metrics, and a rollback criterion. 'We deployed the new rule and alerts went up' is not an evaluation; 'precision held at 0.8 while recall rose from 0.7 to 0.85 on the labeled set' is. Worked program sketch for your IDS: monthly, pull 5,000 labeled events (1,000 malicious from confirmed incidents and red-team activity, 4,000 benign sampled from production); run the current ruleset; publish precision/recall/F1 and the ROC operating point; quarterly, run the false-negative hunt on 200 sampled benign-closed alerts. That is a detection engineering practice, not a tool purchase — and it is what separates teams that detect from teams that alert. Common mistake: treating detection as a product rather than a process. Products decay (M27's arms race); processes adapt. The statistics in this module are the process's instrumentation.

The labeled set is the hard part — labels are expensive, so be systematic about manufacturing them. Three sources. One: confirmed incidents — every resolved incident's indicators become malicious labels, with timestamps bounding the malicious window. Two: red-team and purple-team activity — schedule it partly to generate labels; every red-team action is a known-malicious event with ground truth, the cheapest high-quality labels you will ever get. Three: benign sampling with verification — randomly sample production events and have analysts verify a subset as benign (this is also your false-negative hunt). Maintain the set like code: versioned, with provenance per label (who labeled, from what evidence, when), and refreshed — last year's labels decay as traffic and threats shift. Size guidance: enough malicious samples that a 5-point recall change is statistically meaningful (hundreds, not dozens). And keep a held-out portion the detection engineers never see — evaluate on it, or you are measuring memorization. A detection program without a maintained labeled set is flying blind with extra steps; with one, every tuning decision becomes a measurement.

notes.body:
Machine learning is linear algebra at scale, so we build the objects by hand before they get big. A vector is an ordered list of numbers — [1,2,3] — which you can read two ways: as a point in space (coordinates) or as an arrow from the origin (direction and magnitude). Both readings matter: features of a network event (packet count, byte count, duration) form a vector, and the classifier treats it as a point to be separated or a direction to be measured. Two operations. Addition is component-wise: [1,2,3] + [4,5,6] = [1+4, 2+5, 3+6] = [5,7,9] — geometrically, place the arrows head-to-tail. Scalar multiplication scales every component: 2 × [1,2,3] = [2,4,6] — same direction, twice as long (negative scalars reverse direction). Worked security example: an event's feature vector is [packets=120, bytes=84000, duration_s=60]. Normalize crudely by dividing by [1000, 100000, 3600]... component-wise division isn't a vector operation, but scaling is: (1/1000)×[120, 84000, 60] is not right either — the honest move is scaling each feature to comparable ranges before ML, because raw features with wildly different scales (bytes vs seconds) let the biggest number dominate every distance computation. That preprocessing step — putting features on comparable scales — is applied linear algebra, and skipping it is the most common 'the model doesn't work' root cause in ML-for-security projects. The zero vector [0,0,0] is the origin; subtracting vectors gives the displacement between points: [4,5,6]−[1,2,3] = [3,3,3]. Keep both readings (point and arrow) alive: 'distance between events' uses the point reading, 'direction of change' uses the arrow reading. Common mistake: treating vectors as mere lists. The operations — add, scale, dot (next note) — are what make them vectors; a list you never add or dot is just storage.

Feature engineering is vector design, and it is where security ML is won or lost. Worked: you are building a detector for suspicious PowerShell. Raw input: the command string. Features you might extract: length (characters), entropy of the string, count of suspicious tokens (IEX, DownloadString, -EncodedCommand), number of special characters, max token length. One command becomes [length=212, entropy=4.8, sus_tokens=3, special=31, max_tok=44] — a 5D vector. Two commands' vectors can now be dotted, distanced, and classified. The design decisions are the modeling: including entropy captures obfuscation; counting specific tokens captures known-bad patterns; normalizing (length/1000, entropy/8) keeps scales comparable. Bad features (process ID, timestamp) add noise dimensions the classifier must learn to ignore — and in high dimensions, noise is where evasion lives. The discipline: every feature needs a reason ('obfuscated commands have high entropy'), documented with the vector schema. When the detector fails, the first suspect is the features, not the algorithm. Vectors are the interface between your domain knowledge and the math — design them deliberately.
notes.title: Vectors: points, arrows, and feature vectors

notes.body:
The dot product is the single most-used operation in machine learning — attention mechanisms, similarity search, and classifier scores are all dot products wearing costumes. Definition: a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ — multiply component-wise, add up. Worked: [1,2,3]·[4,5,6] = 1×4 + 2×5 + 3×6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. Geometric meaning: a·b = |a||b|cos θ — the product of lengths times the cosine of the angle between them. So the dot product measures alignment: large positive means the vectors point the same way, zero means perpendicular, negative means opposed. This gives cosine similarity, the workhorse of embeddings and document comparison: cos θ = (a·b)/(|a|·|b|), where |a| = √(a·a) is the length. Worked: a=[1,2,3], b=[4,5,6]. |a| = √(1+4+9) = √14 ≈ 3.742. |b| = √(16+25+36) = √77 ≈ 8.775. cos θ = 32/(3.742×8.775) = 32/32.83 ≈ 0.975 — nearly parallel, strongly aligned. Cosine similarity ignores magnitude: [1,1] and [100,100] have cosine 1.0 — same direction, different sizes. That is a feature for text ('long document about malware' vs 'short note about malware' share direction) and a trap for security features (a 10-packet scan and a 10,000-packet flood point the same way but are very different events — normalize or use Euclidean distance when magnitude matters). Worked security example: compare two process behavior vectors — process A: [file_writes=5, net_conns=2, registry_edits=8], process B: [50, 20, 80]. Cosine similarity: dot = 250+40+640 = 930; |A| = √(25+4+64)=√93≈9.64; |B| = √(2500+400+6400)=√9300≈96.44; cos = 930/(9.64×96.44) = 930/929.7 ≈ 1.0 — identical behavior shape at different scale (B does everything 10× more). An analyst sees 'same pattern, scaled up' — possibly the same malware family with a loop count change. Common mistake: using cosine similarity when magnitude is the signal. Choose the similarity to match the question: direction → cosine; position → Euclidean distance.

Here is why dot products run modern AI: attention is dot-product similarity. In a transformer, each token asks 'which other tokens should I pay attention to?' by dotting its query vector against every token's key vector — high dot product means high relevance, and the softmax turns those scores into weights. Conceptually it is the same operation as your [1,2,3] dot [4,5,6] = 32, scaled to thousands of dimensions and millions of pairs. The security relevance is twofold. First, interpretability: attention weights show what the model 'looked at' — when your AI triage copilot summarizes an alert, attention patterns (where available) hint at which inputs drove the output, a debugging aid for hallucinations. Second, cost: attention is quadratic in sequence length (every token dots every other), which is why long-context inference is expensive and why prompt-injection via long pasted content has a compute cost to the attacker too. You do not need the transformer math — you need the recognition: when a paper or vendor says 'attention-based,' read 'dot-product similarity deciding what matters.' The humble dot product, all the way down.
notes.title: Dot products, angles, and cosine similarity

notes.body:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers — and the operation that matters, matrix multiplication, is just batched dot products. If A is m×n and B is n×p, then C = AB is m×p with C[i,j] = (row i of A)·(column j of B). The inner dimensions must match (n=n); the outer dimensions give the result shape. Worked — the full 2×3 times 3×2, every cell: A = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], B = [[7,8],[9,10],[11,12]]. C[1,1] = [1,2,3]·[7,9,11] = 7+18+33 = 58. C[1,2] = [1,2,3]·[8,10,12] = 8+20+36 = 64. C[2,1] = [4,5,6]·[7,9,11] = 28+45+66 = 139. C[2,2] = [4,5,6]·[8,10,12] = 32+50+72 = 154. Result: [[58,64],[139,154]] ✓. Verify one cell independently: 4×7=28, 5×9=45, 6×11=66, sum 139 ✓. Why this operation runs the world: a neural-network layer computes y = Wx + b — the weight matrix W times the input vector x, plus bias. A batch of inputs is a matrix X, and the layer computes WX + b in one shot — thousands of dot products, perfectly parallel, which is exactly what GPUs were built for. Training is also matrix multiplication (gradients flow through the same products backwards). So 'ML at scale' is, computationally, giant matrix multiplications — the math you just did by hand, billions of times per second. Two properties with teeth. Non-commutativity: AB ≠ BA in general — order matters because matrices are transformations and transformations compose in order (rotate-then-scale ≠ scale-then-rotate). Associativity: (AB)C = A(BC) — regroup freely, which is how inference engines reorder products for speed. Identity: AI = IA = A, where I has ones on the diagonal. Worked non-commutativity check: [[1,1],[0,1]]×[[1,0],[1,1]] = [[2,1],[1,1]], but reversed [[1,0],[1,1]]×[[1,1],[0,1]] = [[1,1],[1,2]] — different. Common mistake: multiplying in the wrong order in code (Wx vs xW) — the dimension check (inner match) catches it instantly. Always check dimensions before debugging values.

The batch dimension is where matrices pay for themselves operationally. Scoring one event is a vector dot product; scoring a million events is a matrix multiplication — same math, but the matrix form lets the hardware (GPUs, vector units) parallelize across all million at once instead of looping. The performance difference is not incremental: batched matrix ops run orders of magnitude faster than equivalent Python loops, which is why 'vectorize your code' is the first optimization in every ML pipeline. Worked sense of scale: a layer with a 1024x512 weight matrix scoring a batch of 256 events is one 1024x512x256 multiplication — 134M multiply-adds, executed in milliseconds on a GPU. This shapes system design: collect events into batches for scoring (throughput over latency), size batches to the hardware, and understand that real-time single-event scoring pays the unbatched price. It also shapes attacks: adversarial ML at scale is batched too — the attacker's gradient computations are matrix products, which is why evasion research iterates fast. The matrix is not just notation; it is the unit of computation the entire stack — math, hardware, and economics — is built around.
notes.title: Matrices: batched dot products that run the world

notes.body:
Norms measure size; distances measure separation — together they turn 'unusual' into a number. The L2 (Euclidean) norm is the straight-line length: |v| = √(Σvᵢ²). The L1 (Manhattan) norm sums absolute values: |v|₁ = Σ|vᵢ|. Worked: v=[3,4]. L2 = √(9+16) = √25 = 5. L1 = 3+4 = 7. L2 is the geometry you picture; L1 is the 'city blocks' distance and is more robust to outliers (one huge component dominates L2's square, less so L1's sum). Euclidean distance between points is the L2 norm of their difference: d(a,b) = |a−b|. Worked: a=[1,2], b=[4,6]. a−b = [−3,−4]; |[−3,−4]| = √(9+16) = 5. These are the primitives of anomaly detection: k-nearest-neighbors flags points far from their neighbors; clustering groups nearby points; thresholds on distance-to-centroid catch outliers. Worked security example: baseline a server's hourly feature vectors (connections, bytes, failed logins) for a month; compute the centroid (mean vector) and the typical distance from it. Tonight's vector sits at 6× the typical distance — investigate. That is statistical anomaly detection in one paragraph, and every refinement (Mahalanobis distance, which corrects for feature correlations; z-scores per feature) is a sophistication of this idea. Normalization connects back to the vector note: if bytes range over millions and failed logins over tens, Euclidean distance is 99.99% 'bytes distance' — standardize each feature (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) so distances reflect shape, not scale. The unit sphere matters too: cosine similarity (previous note) is the dot product of L2-normalized vectors — normalizing to length 1 isolates direction from magnitude. Common mistake: computing distances on unnormalized mixed-scale features and wondering why the detector only sees the biggest feature. Normalize first, distance second — always.

Norms also regularize training — penalizing large weights to keep models simple. L2 regularization adds the squared weight norm to the loss: the optimizer prefers small weights spread across features, which smooths the decision boundary (and, not coincidentally, larger margins — the robustness connection again: L2-regularized models tend to be harder to evade because their boundaries sit farther from the data). L1 regularization adds the absolute norm: it drives unneeded weights exactly to zero, performing feature selection — the model tells you which features it actually uses. Worked intuition: with L1, a 100-feature model might keep 12 nonzero weights — you have learned that 88 features were noise, which is a finding about your data, not just your model. The security angle: inspect the surviving features. If your malware detector's L1 survivors are 'file size' and 'compile timestamp' rather than behavioral features, it is keying on spurious correlations — brittle against trivial attacker changes (recompile, pad the file). Regularization is thus also an audit tool: the weights the model keeps reveal what it learned, and what it learned had better be robust.
notes.title: Norms and distances: measuring 'unusual'

notes.body:
Embeddings are the idea that made modern ML work on language, and the intuition is pure geometry: represent items as dense vectors such that closeness in space means similarity in meaning. 'Dense' matters — unlike one-hot vectors (a million-dimensional vector with a single 1, where every word is equally far from every other), embeddings pack meaning into a few hundred dimensions where geometry works. The similarity measure is usually cosine similarity: similar items point the same way. Worked toy example in 2D — word vectors: malware=[0.9,0.1], ransomware=[0.85,0.15], kitten=[0.1,0.9]. cos(malware, ransomware): dot = 0.9×0.85 + 0.1×0.15 = 0.765+0.015 = 0.78. |malware| = √(0.81+0.01) = √0.82 ≈ 0.9055. |ransomware| = √(0.7225+0.0225) = √0.745 ≈ 0.8631. cos = 0.78/(0.9055×0.8631) = 0.78/0.7816 ≈ 0.998 — nearly identical direction: the model learned they mean nearly the same thing. cos(malware, kitten): dot = 0.9×0.1+0.1×0.9 = 0.18. |kitten| = √0.82 ≈ 0.9055. cos = 0.18/(0.9055×0.9055) = 0.18/0.82 ≈ 0.22 — nearly unrelated. Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions and subtler geometry (king−man+woman≈queen is the famous party trick — vector arithmetic capturing analogies), but the principle is this toy: direction encodes meaning. Security applications: embed process behaviors, log templates, or binaries, then nearest-neighbor search finds 'things like this known-bad thing' — malware family clustering, phishing template matching, and UEBA all use this shape. Two cautions from earlier modules: embeddings are learned from data, so poisoned training data poisons the geometry (M25/M27); and similarity is not identity — 0.998 similar is not 'the same,' so embedding matches are triage leads, not verdicts. Common mistake: treating embedding distance as a probability or a proof. It is a similarity score — useful for ranking and clustering, never a verdict on its own.

Embeddings have their own adversarial angle, and it connects the module's threads. Because embeddings are learned, they are poisonable: slip crafted samples into training and the geometry shifts — the attacker's malware lands near 'benign' clusters. Because similarity is computed by dot product, they are evadable: small input perturbations move the embedding vector across a nearest-neighbor boundary, so 'nearest known-malware' becomes 'nearest benign utility.' And because embedding spaces are dense and high-dimensional, the attacker has room: the curse of dimensionality means tiny pushes find crossings. Defenses mirror the general toolkit: train embeddings on trusted data, monitor the geometry (has the benign cluster drifted?), and never let a nearest-neighbor match be the verdict — it is a triage lead corroborated by independent signals. There is also a privacy angle: embeddings can leak training data (inversion attacks reconstruct inputs from vectors), so treat stored embeddings of sensitive data with the same care as the data. Geometry is powerful, learned, and attackable — the module's refrain, one last time.
notes.title: Embeddings: similarity as geometry

notes.body:
Now the payoff: the linear classifier from M27's evasion lab, understood geometrically. A linear classifier scores s(x) = w·x + b and predicts positive when s > 0. The decision boundary is where the score is zero: w·x + b = 0. In 2D with w=[1,1], b=−3: x₁+x₂−3=0, i.e., the line x₁+x₂=3 — everything above-right scores positive, below-left negative. The weight vector w is perpendicular to the boundary (it points in the direction of steepest score increase — the gradient direction the M27 attacker followed). The margin — a point's perpendicular distance to the boundary — is |w·x+b|/|w|. Worked: x=[2,2]. Score: 1×2+1×2−3 = 1 > 0, positive class. Margin: |1|/√(1²+1²) = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. That 0.707 is the robustness budget: any perturbation with a component larger than 0.707 along −w flips the verdict — and M27's δ=[−0.6,−0.6] (norm ≈0.85) spent exactly that budget. Geometry explains the attack completely: the point sat 0.707 from the line, the attacker pushed 0.85 toward it, the point crossed. Support vector machines make the margin the explicit objective: choose the boundary maximizing the minimum margin over training points — the fattest possible street between the classes. Larger margins mean costlier evasion; that is the geometric reason adversarial training (which effectively pushes points away from the boundary) helps. In higher dimensions the boundary is a hyperplane — same equation, w·x+b=0, with w having one component per feature — and the margin formula is unchanged. The 'curse' from M27 also geometric: in high dimensions, most of a point's neighborhood lies near some boundary direction, so small perturbations find crossings easily. Worked 3D extension: w=[1,−1,0.5], b=0, x=[2,1,2]. Score: 2−1+1 = 2 > 0. Margin: 2/√(1+1+0.25) = 2/1.5 ≈ 1.333. Same mechanics, one more dimension. Common mistake: thinking the boundary is where the data is. The boundary is where the model is maximally uncertain — the most attackable real estate in the feature space, which is why attackers live there.

Do not overlook b, the bias term — geometrically it is the boundary's offset from the origin, and operationally it is the prior baked into the model. With b = 0, the boundary passes through the origin: the classifier is 'fair' between classes at the origin. Our b = -3 shifted the line outward: at the origin (x = [0,0]), the score is -3, confidently negative — the model defaults to negative unless the features push hard positive. That default is a choice with consequences: in detection terms, b encodes the tradeoff between false positives and false negatives before any feature is even considered. Raising b (less negative) moves the boundary toward the negative class — more positives, higher recall, more false alarms: it is the threshold knob from statistics, inside the equation. When you inherit a model, inspect b (and the score distribution): a model with an extreme bias is really a mostly-constant classifier wearing a linear costume. And when you train, remember the bias learns the class balance of the training data — train on 99%-benign data and the bias absorbs that prior, which is correct for that population and wrong everywhere else. The bias is the base rate, smuggled into geometry.
notes.title: How a linear classifier draws its line

notes.body:
One more geometric idea, because it powers real anomaly detection: dimensionality reduction and the intuition behind eigenvectors. Real security data has hundreds of features, but the interesting variation often lives in far fewer directions. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds those directions: the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, ordered by eigenvalue (variance captured). Intuition without the full derivation: imagine points scattered mostly along a diagonal line with small perpendicular jitter. The first principal component points along the diagonal (the direction of greatest spread); the second points perpendicular (the jitter direction). Projecting onto just the first component compresses 2D to 1D while keeping the shape that matters. The anomaly-detection trick: learn the principal components of normal traffic, then for each new point measure reconstruction error — project it onto the top components and back, and see how much was lost. Normal points reconstruct well (they fit the learned shape); anomalies reconstruct poorly (they stick out in directions normal data doesn't use). Worked sketch: normal SSH sessions cluster with (bytes, duration) along a line — big transfers take longer. A session with huge bytes and tiny duration reconstructs badly → flag: possible exfiltration-shaped anomaly. That is PCA anomaly detection in a paragraph; your lab implements the core (find the max-variance direction by search). Eigenvectors generally: Av = λv — directions a matrix stretches without rotating, scaled by λ. They appear wherever linear transformations repeat: covariance matrices (PCA), graph adjacency (network centrality — nodes important because important nodes link to them), and Markov chains. You don't need to compute eigendecompositions by hand; you need the intuition — 'the natural axes of the data' — so that when a paper says 'we projected onto the top-k principal components,' you picture the diagonal line, not a black box. And the security caveat, on brand for this course: PCA learns 'normal' from training data — poison that data (M27) and the learned normal includes the attacker's shape. Geometry is powerful, and like every model, it trusts its training data. Common mistake: keeping too few components and discarding the signal, or too many and keeping the noise. The eigenvalue spectrum (how fast variance drops off) tells you where to cut.

Eigenvectors have a second security life beyond PCA: graphs. A network's adjacency matrix has a principal eigenvector — and its entries are eigenvector centrality: nodes score highly when connected to other high-scoring nodes. Worked intuition: in a corporate network graph, the domain controller has high centrality (everything talks to it); a workstation that suddenly jumps in centrality is worth investigating — what is it suddenly connected to? Attack-path analysis uses the same math: the attacker's lateral movement follows high-centrality paths, and defenders harden the nodes whose removal fragments the graph. Even PageRank is an eigenvector computation. The unifying idea: when a matrix describes relationships (covariance between features, adjacency between hosts), its eigenvectors reveal the structure's natural axes — the directions along which the system actually varies or connects. Learn to ask 'what are this matrix's eigenvectors?' about any matrix you meet in security tooling, and you will extract insights the raw numbers hide. It is the same question as PCA, asked of a different matrix — which is why the intuition transfers.
